finding.claim: Unauthenticated SSRF: a user-supplied URL in POST 'feed' is fetched server-side with file_get_contents(); the response length is echoed back, giving an oracle on internal responses. No scheme, host, or IP restriction, and no authentication.

trace.note: session_start(); no authorization is applied to this branch
Branch taken when REQUEST_METHOD === 'POST' and isset($_POST['feed']); require_admin() is not called
$_POST['feed'] is passed unvalidated to file_get_contents(), which follows http://, https://, and (if enabled) other stream wrappers, and follows redirects by default
strlen($xml) is echoed, so the attacker learns the size of the fetched body (a length oracle for internal services)

finding.guards_checked: No authentication/session check on this branch (require_admin is only on line 18). No scheme allowlist, hostname/IP allowlist, private/loopback/link-local range block, port restriction, or redirect limit. No input type or length validation. Note: file_get_contents also accepts file:// and php:// wrappers when allowed, which widens impact beyond SSRF (local file read, though only the length is returned here).

verdict.guard_found: none. Line 11 gates the branch only on REQUEST_METHOD and isset($_POST['feed']); require_admin() (import.php:4-9) is called only at line 18, outside this branch. Line 12 passes $_POST['feed'] to file_get_contents with no scheme, host, IP, or redirect validation.
verdict.reason: import.php:11 takes the branch for any unauthenticated POST containing 'feed', and import.php:12 passes that attacker-controlled value straight to file_get_contents(), with the length echoed at import.php:13 and no closing guard anywhere on the path.

finding.claim: Admin-gated SSRF: the 'set_webhook' parameter is used as the URL for a server-side cURL request. The response body is discarded, so the attack is blind (fire-and-forget), but it can still reach internal hosts and trigger side-effecting GET/POST requests.
finding.source: import.php:19 $_POST['set_webhook'] (HTTP POST parameter, attacker-controlled only if the attacker holds an admin session or can make an admin's browser send the request)
finding.sink: import.php:20 curl_init($hook), executed at import.php:22 curl_exec($ch)

trace.note: require_admin() checks empty($_SESSION['is_admin']) and returns 403 if not set
curl_init($hook) creates a handle for the attacker-supplied URL
CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER set, but the result is never output
curl_exec($ch) sends the request; the response is discarded and not returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: require_admin() session check at import.php:18 (empty($_SESSION['is_admin'])); this is the only guard. No URL scheme allowlist, host/IP block, or CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS restriction. CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION is not set, so redirects are not followed. The admin check is outside this file, so how is_admin is set and whether the session is protected from fixation or CSRF could not be verified from this code alone. Severity is lower than SSRF-1 because it requires admin privilege and the response is blind.

verdict.guard_found: require_admin() at import.php:4-9, which returns 403 unless $_SESSION['is_admin'] is set. This is an authorization gate, not a URL validation. No scheme, host, or IP restriction exists, and CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS is not set.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (import.php:17-22), but the source at import.php:19 is reachable only after the admin check at import.php:18 and line 5 passes, so a low-privilege or unauthenticated attacker cannot control it. The finding depends on an admin session or on CSRF against an admin, and nothing in this code shows a CSRF path, so it does not meet the bar for a remotely attacker-controlled source.
